parts:
Hi there,

Alright, my first time with iRace 2 (after Matheuristics) Have mercy, since my understanding is incomplete, and I am not an R person... :)

Two main questions, which ended up having lots of sub-questions:

1) In your paper, could you please include a figure that sheds some light on the technical terms? I am more a visual person...
This can help to undestand what is happening in the iRace output (iterations/each line/experiment/...).
For example:
- nbIterations (dependent on number of parameters) in the number of "overall" iterations, but what is actually an iteration?
- nbExperimentsPerIteration (looking at page 42 of the guide) is the number of experiments in an iteration, but the default is 0 and it does not seem to be outputed in debug=0, and nbExperimentsPerIteration seems to vary somehow
- nbConfigurations is based on the previous one, but then talks about iterations again :-O
- mu number of configurations sampled...
--> These four confuse me a fair bit. Should I know them since they are adjusted automatically? Maybe not. Do I want to get an intuitive understanding? Yes :)

2) Just double-checking: is the very same seed (intially sampled) the same one used in every experiment?
2.1) Related: in the testing phase (or always?), the configuration(s) are run just once per instance, right? If the algorithm is stochastic, how could I run the configurations x times in the testing phase (or always?) from within iRace?
2.2) In particular in combination with a provided algorithm configuration, the following would be super helpful: run the given configuration(s) x=50 times on the testing/training/complete set, then run the final top elitist (or top n=3) on the same set(s), and then provide all the plots automatically (or at least the average) ;) Of course I can do this myself externally based on the framework's outputs, but the framework is already so close to providing these steps.

3) Below is one output and one config file. Do you think the iRace output looks okay to you? My question is just about a sanity check of the iRace configuration used - I'll interpret the actual numbers after the optimisation.
Yes, I have only a single parameter right now, CANDCOUNT=(1,1000), with small values most likely being best, and the problem instances' outcomes are in a wide range. I am using iRace 2.1.1662 under linux.

Cheers,
Markus

messages.subject: Re: assorted questions: technical terms, seeds, example run
parts:
On Thursday, 3 November 2016 06:23:40 UTC, Markus Wagner wrote:
Hi there,

Welcome Markus
Alright, my first time with iRace 2 (after Matheuristics) Have mercy, since my understanding is incomplete, and I am not an R person... :)
You should not need to be an R person to use irace! If you need to, there is a bug ;-)

Two main questions, which ended up having lots of sub-questions:

1) In your paper, could you please include a figure that sheds some light on the technical terms? I am more a visual person...

By "paper", do you mean the "user guide" (vignette) ?

I think the workings of irace are more clearly described in the actual paper:

Manuel López-Ibáñez, Jérémie Dubois-Lacoste, Leslie Pérez Cáceres, Thomas Stützle, and Mauro Birattari. The irace package: Iterated Racing for Automatic Algorithm Configuration. Operations Research Perspectives, 3:43-58, 2016.<doi:10.1016/j.orp.2016.09.002>

This can help to undestand what is happening in the iRace output (iterations/each line/experiment/...).
For example:
- nbIterations (dependent on number of parameters) in the number of "overall" iterations, but what is actually an iteration?

An iteration is generation of solutions + racing to select the best. I have extended the definition in the user guide to say:

nbIterations flag: --iterations default: 0
Number of iterations to be executed. Each iteration involves the generation of new con-
figurations and the use of racing to select the best configurations. By default (with 0),
irace calculates the number of iterations as N^iter = 2 + log2 N^param, where N param is the
number of non fixed parameters to be tuned. We recommend to use the default value.

Is it clear now?

- nbExperimentsPerIteration (looking at page 42 of the guide) is the number of experiments in an iteration, but the default is 0 and it does not seem to be outputed in debug=0, and nbExperimentsPerIteration seems to vary somehow

There (11.3) it explains what happens for the default value (but we failed to say that '0' means use the automatic way, fixed now). Basically, by default irace reserves a maximum amount of budget per iteration that depends on the budget left and the iteration number. Better not to touch it, unless you are really prepared to think about the consequences (the iteration budget determines the number of configurations present in the iteration, too many and you are doing random search, too little and you cannot sample anything new and irace will stop).
- nbConfigurations is based on the previous one, but then talks about iterations again :-O

By default, the number of configurations (the population size if irace was an EA) is dynamic and depends on the budget left and on the minimum number of instances that should be seen at each iteration. The latter increases at each iteration (because one wants to be more and more confident that the best solution is actually the best). Could you explain what is not understandable in the explanation? It would be good if we could improve it.
- mu number of configurations sampled...

Actually, it says: "This value is used to determine the number of configurations to be sampled
  and evaluated at each iteration", so it is not exactly the number of configurations (as can be seen in the formula). But I have extended the explanation as follows:

"The number of configurations will be calculated such that there is enough budget in each race to evaluate all of
  them on at least $\mu + \min(5,j)$ training instances, where $j$ is the index
  of the current iteration. The value of $\mu$ will be adjusted to never be
  lower than the value of \parameter{firstTest}. See also \parameter{firstTest}
  and \parameter{eachTest}."

Is the above clearer?
--> These four confuse me a fair bit. Should I know them since they are adjusted automatically? Maybe not. Do I want to get an intuitive understanding? Yes :)

If you just wish to use irace, you don't need to know them and things may not work as expected if you start to change them arbitrarily. They are designed so that you can play with the budget and with firstTest, which are much more important parameters, and the rest will be adjusted automatically.
2) Just double-checking: is the very same seed (intially sampled) the same one used in every experiment?

There is a paragraph regarding this:

By default, \irace assumes that the target algorithm is stochastic (the value
of the option \parameter{deterministic} is $0$), thus, the same configuration
can be executed more than once on the same instance and obtain different
results.  In this case, \irace generates pairs \code{(instance, seed)} by
generating a random seed for each instance. Once all pairs have been seen within
a run of \irace, new pairs are generated with different seeds.

Of course, the seed provided with --seed controls the other seeds generated, so that you can reproduce your run of irace (if the target-algorithm/computation environment is also reproducible). Is the above clear?
 
2.1) Related: in the testing phase (or always?), the configuration(s) are run just once per instance, right? If the algorithm is stochastic, how could I run the configurations x times in the testing phase (or always?) from within iRace?2.2) In particular in combination with a provided algorithm configuration, the following would be super helpful: run the given configuration(s) x=50 times on the testing/training/complete set, then run the final top elitist (or top n=3) on the same set(s), and then provide all the plots automatically (or at least the average) ;) Of course I can do this myself externally based on the framework's outputs, but the framework is already so close to providing these steps.

As long as there are enough training instances, irace will not run any configuration more than once on each training instance. The rationale for this is given here:

http://www.metaheuristics.net/~mbiro/paperi/IridiaTr2004-001r004.pdf

But it can be intuitively understood if you think about the two extreme cases. If you want to estimate the expected performance of an algorithm on a problem defined as a (possibly infinite) set of unseen instances (e.g., all Euclidean TSP instances), will you base your estimation on N runs on 1 instance or 1 run on N instances? The above paper shows mathematically that any trade-off between these two cases is still a worse estimator than 1-run-N-instances.

If at some moment, irace wants to do another evaluation, but it runs out of instances, then irace will start repeating instances but using a different random seed for them.

As for the testing phase, following the above, irace does only one run for each instance that you provide. The testing instances do not influence the selection of the best (otherwise they will not be 'testing' instances). They are just a way for you to check for overtuning. Thus, you are free to add both training and testing as testing instances and separate them a posteriori, duplicate instances in order to get as many replicates as you wish to have, etc. (Unfortunately, there is a little bug in irace 2.1 that will evaluate a testing instance only once even if it appears two times in the testInstanceFile, but this was not intended and it will be fixed in 2.2. I can send you a pre-release version in private if you wish).

Of course, if you want to always do 100 runs, you can do this in target-runner and report to irace just the mean (or the median or the worst or the 25% percentile or...).

To run the final top 3, you would use --testNbElites 3.

As for the plots, what plots would you like to get automatically? A boxplot of the configurations tested at the end? This is as simple as doing:

load("irace.Rdata")
boxplot(iraceResults$testing$experiments)

but I'm afraid it would be difficult to generate automatically a boxplot that looks nice for everybody. Nevertheless, if you think the above would be useful, we could add an option that generates such plots automatically.

3) Below is one output and one config file. Do you think the iRace output looks okay to you? My question is just about a sanity check of the iRace configuration used - I'll interpret the actual numbers after the optimisation.
Yes, I have only a single parameter right now, CANDCOUNT=(1,1000), with small values most likely being best, and the problem instances' outcomes are in a wide range. I am using iRace 2.1.1662 under linux.

It looks fine to me. Some tips that could be useful:

* If you have numerical parameters with a wide range and you think that their effect will be more pronounced on one side than on the other (that is, the difference between 1 and 2 is larger than the difference between 999 and 1000), then you may wish to tune a transformation of the parameter (such as logarithmic scaling). Doing this transformation automatically is in the TODO list, but it is trivial to do the scaling yourself in your target-runner. Another example is tuning a real value such as [0.000001, 1], where what matters most is the difference between 0.000001 and 0.00001 rather than between 0.9 and 1. Then, it may be better to tune a numerical parameter [-6,0] and compute 10^p within the target-runner. Of course, all this is scenario specific and one may not know what is best a priori.

* Since the output values have such different ranges for each instance, you have to decide how you evaluate the overall performance of your algorithm. Imagine you have two algorithms A and B:

A      B
100  1
1     10
1    10
1   10
1   10
1   10

If you are only interested in the mean value, then B is better. If you are interested in the ranking, then A is better. The default settings of irace look at rankings, which are less sensitive to outliers and instances with different ranges. Using --test-type t-test optimizes specifically the overall mean (but then the ranges used in your training instances become very important). Another alternative is that, if you know the optimal/best-known for each instance, your target-runner could return instead the relative percentage deviation or some normalized value for each instance.

I hope the above is useful.

Cheers,

Manuel.

parts:
> ps: the user guide link at the bottom
> of http://iridia.ulb.ac.be/irace/ contains an unnecessary “." at the end, I think.
Good catch! Many thanks. Fixed now.

> As your technology will hopefully be used widely across many fields, having it
> more “self-contained” should be helpful for others.

My worry is that we do not want the user-guide to duplicate the journal paper.
One should not need to understand how irace works to just use it. We do expose
some internal options that some researchers may wish to play with, specially if
they wish to improve irace itself.

Another point against precisely explaining the defaults is that they are a bit
complicated, some of them for practical reasons, some of them for historical
reasons. The journal paper is pretty extensive about it and we may end up
summarising too much or introducing mistakes if we try to duplicate this
information in the user-guide. In fact, some of the equations mentioned in the
current user-guide are not correct for the elitist version, which is now the
default in 2.0. The correct details are in the journal paper.

Nevertheless, I agree that we should give at least an informal description of
irace with the help of some figures. And perhaps further clarify the separation
between user-facing options and internal options. Moreover, one should not need
to read the journal paper to understand the output of irace, thus if you find
something there that you think is confusing or an internal detail, please let
us now and we'll move it under the --debug option.

Cheers,
Manuel.

messages.subject: Re: [irace-package] assorted questions: technical terms, seeds, example run
parts:
> Since I had only two iterations in my scenario, I wondered what kind of
> optimisation can happen in just two iterations. And then I varied the budget so
> widely and still ended up with only two iterations... In combination with the
> additional explanations and the ORP article, this is clearer now.

The ancestor of irace, Iterated F-race, defined the number of iterations in
such a way that, with only 1 parameter, you get only 2 iterations. Normally,
one would have budget left after the two iterations and irace will continue
doing more iterations. In my humble opinion, this default is not ideal, but we
would need to replace it with something clearly better, not just different. And
this is trickier than it sounds, because it has to work on the really
interesting scenarios. Tuning only 1 parameter is really not very interesting
(and not that common in our applications), thus we haven't been motivated to
explore different defaults.

> Yes. For those externals who are not reading the ORP article: why do you need
> iterations? (I mean: what happens from one to the next?)

We need to know the iterations to plan how to spend the budget. Between one
iteration and the next, some configurations are discarded and the sampling
distribution from which new configurations are sampled becomes more restricted
towards the best configurations found so far. Similar to ACO, EDA and
reinforcement learning.

> Okay, I missed the thorough understanding of the following terms:
> configuration, racing, iteration, evaluation, experiment… I just could not
> quickly build the correct hierarchy in my head of what influences which aspect,
> and then they change over time… I am happy to use iRace largely as a black box,
> but I want to be able to interpret logfiles :)

Please, do not hesitate to complain about anything that is not clear in the
logfiles or the user-guide. We have been trying to make terms and concepts more
consistent and to follow the consensus in the wider automatic algorithm
configuration community (if you see the NEWS file for 2.0, we have renamed a
lot of options, files, etc.) But surely, there is more to be done. We also have
a glossary in Appendix C that should grow over time as users give us feedback
about what to include there.

> Can you please provide an intuition behind the impact of firstTest and
> eachTest? I see “Specifies how many instances are evaluated before the first
> elimination test. “ and “Specifies how many instances are evaluated between
> elimination tests. “, but the intuition does not come to me easily.

I think we need to extend Section 10.4 (Heterogeneous scenarios) and make a
reference to it from the list of options.

Basically, if you increase firstTest, irace will evaluate each configuration on
more instances before discarding them for the first time. This is useful if you
know that you have very heterogeneous instances in your problem and discarding
configurations without seeing enough instances may strongly bias the result
towards one class (or produce a configuration that fails catastrophically on
some instances). Higher values produce more robust configurations at the cost
of exploring fewer configurations.

For example, recently I tuned an algorithm for which some parameter
configurations will produce very consistent results, whether other
configurations will produce even better results but a terrible result in 10% of
the runs. I wanted to make sure I didn't get the latter configurations, so I
cranked up firstTest to 15 (10 was perhaps enough, but just to be sure).

eachTest controls how big of a block of instances is seen between additional
tests. If you know that you have precisely 5 heterogeneous classes of
instances, you may wish to set this value to 5 or more, to reduce the bias of
any particular class. One can also disable samplesInstances and setup the
trainInstancesFile to present blocks of 5 instances, one of each class, to
irace. In such a scenario, firstTest will be some multiple of 5 (35 or 50) and
eachTest would be 5. This will help to produce a configuration that performs
well over all classes at once.

> Since I do not immediate see it in the paper: what if I can do more than N runs
> in total? Let’s say 10*N, or N^2, or so? What is then the best combination?

The best combination is to always use all instances that you have, and then do
as many replications of all instances as you can. However, statistically
speaking, since additional replications on the same instance are not truly
independent, some statistical tests that assume independence start to
misbehave. We actually do not pay attention in irace to this potential issue
because we only use the statistics as a greedy selection, but Felipe Campelo
and I are currently investigating what may be its real impact for irace and, if
any, how to alleviate it.

Cheers,

Manuel.

messages.subject: Re: [irace-package] assorted questions: technical terms, seeds, example run
parts:
On 08/11/16 01:04, Markus Wagner wrote:
>> However, statistically speaking, since additional replications on the same instance are not truly independent,
>
> Can you explain this please? You mean because the random number generator is using timeInMilliseconds, and thus two replications are not independent?

Roughly speaking, it follows from the fact that data from 1 run on 2*N
instances is more informative than data from 2 runs on N instances. A
statistical test may assume that in both cases you have 2*N independent data
points, but in the latter case there is actually less information than in the
former. This is because the 2 runs on the same instance gives you more
information about how the algorithm may behave on that precise instance but
less information than 1 run on 2 instances about how it will behave on a
yet-unseen instance of the same problem.

On Thursday, 10 November 2016 00:05:44 UTC, Markus Wagner wrote:

By the way, I saw that seeds get reused a lot across one instance (see screenshot below, where 997723759 is the seed) while the parameter (rightmost column only) gets changed. Assuming that the paramer has an impact on the algorithm's behaviour, using the same random seed is fine of course. I wonder: reusing the seed was more of a software design decision or is there some theoretical justification for it as well?

Our seeds are randomly generated per instance, and, if the same configuration is evaluated twice on the same instance, each evaluation uses a different seed. Intuitively, using the same seed for the same instance should reduce spurious variance by, for example, making the initial population or solution the same. This is an intuition with which several experienced people on empirical algorithm analysis seem to agree, and the results that we got when we changed this (in 1.07) were positive, but I don't have any theoretical paper that I can cite to justify this. And I will don't hesitate to change it if it turned out to be the wrong intuition. I can also see intuitively that, taking this to the extreme, that is, if one always uses the same fixed seeds (something like 1,2,3,4... or even a single seed) for all instances, one can end up measuring some spurious effects () that would be very rare if the seed was really random for every run.

parts:
On Wednesday, 9 November 2016 23:05:12 UTC, Markus Wagner wrote:
One more question: based on your experience, how many experiments should one run given 100 instances and 1 integer parameter?

As I said above, the way irace works right now, it doesn't matter how many training instances you have and how much budget you give to irace, irace will only use those instances that it needs to discard configurations. Thus, adding more instances or more budget does not mean that more instances will be used. How many instances are used only depends on how easy/hard is to discard configurations. You'll need to play with firstTest/eachTest to force irace to see more instances before discarding configurations.

I know this depends on lots of factors, so how about the following: do you think x=1000 experiments is okay (goven 100 instances and 1 parameter), or are 1000 still borderline and 10,000 better? Or 100,000? Of course, the more the better... however, where might be an interesting trade-off since computing resources are limited?

There is a check in irace that will compute how many experiments are needed to be able to run at least 2+log_2(nbParameters) iterations of irace. If your budget is too low, it will refuse to run. This is to run at least as many iterations as the original iterated F-race prescribed.

However, there is no rule of thumb at the moment to predict how much budget one needs, since that depends on how good the final configuration needs to be for you to be satisfied, how difficult is to find that configuration, how heterogeneous are the training instances, etc. I'm not even sure where to start in order to investigate such rule of thumb.

If you are interested in obtaining a very good configuration in short time, the way I will do it is to run irace with the budget that will keep the cluster busy until the next time that I can check the results (one night? one weekend?). Look at the final configurations and see if I'm happy with them. if not, but they are better than random/default, then seed the next irace run with these configurations and do another repetition. Repeat the process until happy or you ran out of patience.
